reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 14-1] Appendix D provides a guide specification for drilled shaft construction, adapted primarily from 'Section 5 - Drilled Shafts' of the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Construction Specifications, 4th Edition (AASHTO, 2017b), with provisions from the authors' recent experience and commentary giving guidance and alternative provisions; AASHTO text and commentary are in standard font, supplementary provisions and commentary in italics. It is not intended for direct project use: engineers should develop their own project-focused specification, using Appendix D only as a guide to typical issues and provisions. Other references: Specification for the Construction of Drilled Piers, ACI 336.1-01 (ACI, 2017); Standards and Specifications for the Foundation Drilling Industry (ADSC, 1999); standard specifications of government agencies, including state DOTs. The chapter discusses key topics to consider in any project-specific specification.
key_points: Guide specification in Appendix D, adapted from AASHTO (2017b) Section 5 with authors' provisions (italics)
Not for direct project use; write a project-focused specification
Also consult ACI 336.1-01 (ACI, 2017), ADSC (1999) and state DOT specifications
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft construction specifications on transportation projects

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.body: [pp. 14-1 to 14-2] Drilled shaft nominal resistance and serviceability are influenced by the installation method and the care exercised: poor bottom cleaning may considerably reduce base resistance; prolonged exposure of the excavation sides to slurry may greatly reduce friction resistance; failure to maintain a stable excavation may cause voids or soil inclusions that compromise structural integrity. Unlike driven piles, whose driving resistance assesses each pile, drilled shafts rely on consistent, repeatable application of the installation procedures demonstrated by successful technique shafts (also called trial, demonstration or method shafts) and test shafts. Specifications must emphasize: qualifications of the contractor and key personnel; planning through preparation and review of a Drilled Shaft Installation Plan; methods appropriate to the ground and groundwater; technique shafts to evaluate the contractor's means and methods; load test shafts to verify design assumptions and justify higher resistance factors; integrity testing (Chapter 16); and clearly defined acceptance criteria and installation tolerances.
key_points: Resistance and serviceability depend on installation method and care
Poor base cleaning, long slurry exposure and unstable holes reduce resistance or integrity
No driving-resistance check: rely on repeatable procedures proven by technique and test shafts
Emphasize qualifications, Installation Plan, methods, technique shafts, load tests, integrity testing, acceptance criteria
sections.applicability: Specification development for drilled shaft projects

sections.title: Qualifications of Drilled Shaft Contractors
sections.body: [p. 14-2] Drilled shafts are typically highly loaded and often non-redundant, requiring workmanship only experienced contractors provide: contract documents should require minimum contractor qualifications and, when appropriate, successful technique shaft(s) at the start of construction to demonstrate capabilities and the proposed method in the site conditions, considering the project's risk and complexity (Appendix D suggests requirements for a typical transportation project). Require minimum qualifications for key staff: superintendent, foremen and lead drillers, testing personnel and independent inspectors (design-build). It is generally undesirable for a general contractor to hire a specialty contractor only to excavate while another places steel and/or concrete: added coordination and delay may impact performance and invite disputes over integrity (improper placement or an inappropriate mix?). Excavation, steel and concrete are all critical operations that should typically be performed continuously and coordinated by a single qualified contractor.
key_points: Require minimum contractor qualifications and, when appropriate, technique shafts
Qualify superintendent, foremen, lead drillers, testing personnel, independent inspectors (design-build)
One qualified contractor for excavation, steel and concrete; splitting invites delay and disputes

sections.title: Construction Method
sections.body: [pp. 14-2 to 14-3] Permitted methods (Chapters 3, 4 and 5) must consider ground and groundwater conditions and the design reliance on side resistance, end bearing, or both, which largely determine drilling equipment, wet or dry excavation, drilling fluid, permanent or temporary casing and cleanout criteria; methods and design then influence the concrete mix and placement. For wet excavations the specification must require a concrete mix with the necessary slump or spread range, minimum workability duration and maximum aggregate size suitable for tremie placement. Since many combinations of equipment and procedures can succeed, the specification should not needlessly restrict tools, equipment or method and should permit as much flexibility as project and site constraints allow, but where conditions dictate a method (e.g., wet methods in cohesionless soils below groundwater) general requirements are appropriate.
key_points: Methods follow ground, groundwater and reliance on side and/or base resistance
Wet excavation: specify slump or spread range, workability duration, maximum aggregate size for tremie
Maximize contractor flexibility; dictate methods only where conditions require (e.g., wet method in sands below groundwater)
sections.applicability: Construction method specification; contractor flexibility provisions

sections.title: Drilling Fluid
sections.body: [p. 14-3] Drilling fluid stabilizes the excavation until casing reaches a competent layer or concrete is placed (Chapter 5); the fluid types specified (mineral slurry, polymer slurry or water) should suit the ground and installation method. Monitor and control slurry properties during mixing, during drilling and just before concrete placement. Primary concerns: (1) borehole stability during excavation and concreting; (2) no weakening of the bond between concrete and the shaft side or reinforcement; (3) all slurry displaced by the rising concrete; (4) no sediment deposited in the excavation or rising concrete. Specification provisions: (1) identify fluids that may or may not be used; (2) specify a suitable range of slurry properties during excavation and just before concreting; (3) slurry inspection tests; (4) pre-production technique shaft(s) to evaluate the proposed wet method.
key_points: Fluid type suited to ground and method; control properties at mixing, drilling and before concreting
Concerns: stability, bond, full displacement by concrete, no sediment deposition
Specify permitted fluids, property ranges, inspection tests and technique shafts
sections.applicability: Drilling fluid specification for wet construction

sections.title: Load Testing
sections.body: [pp. 14-3 to 14-4] Load testing (Chapter 13) is often specified for high capacity foundations of major structures, ground where resistance cannot be reliably estimated, and projects with enough shafts to justify the cost. Conventional static tests with dead weight or a reaction frame are generally not practical for high capacity shafts; bi-directional load cell testing is more practical and economical and commonly used, per ASTM D8169/D8169M ('Standard Test Methods for Deep Foundations under Bi-directional Static Axial Compressive Load'), referenced in Appendix D. Rapid compression force pulse tests (ASTM D7383, combustion gas pressure 'Procedure A' or cushioned drop mass 'Procedure B') and high strain dynamic tests (ASTM D4945) estimate resistance from dynamic response and are referenced in Appendix D. Lateral load tests, occasionally performed for lateral response or p-y properties, should follow ASTM D3966/D3966M for the static method; there are at present no standards for bi-directional or rapid lateral tests, so caution is needed in their planning, execution and interpretation.
key_points: Specify load tests for high capacity, uncertain resistance, or many shafts
Bi-directional per ASTM D8169/D8169M; rapid per ASTM D7383 (Procedure A gas, B drop mass); dynamic per ASTM D4945
Static lateral per ASTM D3966/D3966M; no standards for bi-directional or rapid lateral tests
sections.applicability: Load test specification; load test program requirements in contract documents

sections.title: Integrity Testing
sections.body: [pp. 14-4 to 14-5] Shafts can have defects such as necking, bulging, voids, honeycombing and loss of cover, particularly with the wet method, so non-destructive integrity testing (Chapter 16) should generally be part of any project anticipating wet construction and an essential element of all technique and load test shafts; it should not be the sole means of assessing structural adequacy but a key component of the overall QA/QC program with proper design, installation and inspection (Chapter 17). Purposes: at the start of construction to confirm the proposed methods; routinely on all or a defined percentage of production shafts; when means and methods change significantly; to investigate shafts suspected of defects from installation observations; to evaluate remedial measures. Methods (Chapter 16): internal (Cross-hole Sonic Logging, Thermal Integrity Profiling, Gamma-Gamma Density Logging) and external (Sonic Echo, Impulse Response). Appendix D includes CSL provisions (common, and tubes must be installed during construction) and Thermal Integrity Profiling (gaining acceptance); if internal testing is not specified, consider provisions for external testing by a qualified specialist of shafts suspected of defects during concreting. Owner-required methods (e.g., Gamma-Gamma Logging for Caltrans) should be incorporated or referenced.
key_points: Integrity testing for wet-method projects and all technique and load test shafts
Part of QA/QC, not the sole adequacy check (Chapter 17)
Purposes: confirm methods, routine QC/QA, method changes, suspected defects, remediation checks
Appendix D: CSL and Thermal Integrity Profiling; external tests (Sonic Echo, Impulse Response) as fallback
sections.applicability: Specifying integrity testing of drilled shafts

sections.title: Construction Phase Subsurface Investigations
sections.body: [p. 14-5] The design phase investigation (Chapter 2) should suit the design and site, and its data should be referenced or included in the contract documents for responsive bids and to reduce unanticipated conditions and differing site condition claims (Section 2.6). Additional construction-phase investigations may be required: confirmation borings at each non-redundant shaft; shafts in rock to fix socket depth and length at each shaft; highly variable sites not sufficiently defined in design; and commonly design-build contracts, where element locations are set by the design-builder. Requirements typically go in a separate specification section referenced in Drilled Shafts; guidance is in FHWA GEC No. 5 (FHWA-NHI-16-072, Loehr et al., 2017) and Chapter 2.
key_points: Include design phase data in contract documents to limit differing site condition claims
Construction-phase borings: non-redundant shafts, rock socket depths, variable sites, design-build
Separate specification section; guidance in GEC 5 (Loehr et al., 2017)
sections.applicability: Specifying construction-phase subsurface investigations for drilled shafts

sections.title: Drilled Shaft Installation Plan
sections.body: [pp. 14-5 to 14-6] A Drilled Shaft Installation Plan is essential: it communicates installation requirements to construction personnel and inspectors and is the basis for identifying deviations from reviewed equipment and procedures. The contractor prepares it for review by the owner and/or foundation design engineer before any shaft construction; Appendix D lists minimum content. It should be project-specific, not a generic list, fully documenting equipment and procedures so the engineer can confirm compliance and identify practices that may adversely affect nominal resistance or serviceability. The contractor revises and resubmits after review, and work should not proceed until the Plan is accepted; it is updated and resubmitted whenever equipment or procedures change significantly, and field staff should always have the latest approved version.
key_points: Contractor-prepared, project-specific Plan reviewed before any shaft work (minimum content in Appendix D)
No work until accepted; update on significant changes; field staff use the latest version
sections.applicability: Requiring and reviewing a Drilled Shaft Installation Plan

sections.title: Measurement and Payment
sections.body: [pp. 14-6 to 14-8] Unit pricing is typical for design-bid-build, with excavation paid either as unclassified or as separate soil and rock items, the latter preferred and used in Appendix D. Unclassified excavation may suit sites with little or no hard rock, ambiguous transitions to difficult drilling, or agencies reducing administration, but raises bid contingency, partly addressed by a good design-stage investigation made available to bidders. Separate soil and rock payment is equitable for hard rock needing different equipment or slower rates, reduces bid uncertainty and is generally more economical; items should be defined by difficulty and rate, the guide specification suggesting an Unconfined Compressive Strength of 1,000 psi as the division (requiring sufficient strength tests before and during construction); alternatively, some agencies define pay items by equipment (conventional augers and buckets vs. special rock augers, core barrels or other unconventional tools). Separate items need careful definitions, knowledgeable inspectors and coordination on quantities and disputes. Obstructions should be a separate pay item: some agencies pay 2 or 3 times the soil drilling rate per unit depth, some time and materials; a defined obstruction quantity paid only when exceeded shares risk. Washington State DOT (2018) pays an agreed hourly stand-by rate for equipment idled by obstruction removal if it cannot be reassigned. Steel and concrete may be paid by weight and volume or combined per unit length for each diameter; concrete by volume is usually from design dimensions excluding overbreak or unauthorized extra penetration, but where large losses are anticipated (e.g., cavities in karstic rock) a base unit cost with a defined contractual overpour percentage and separate payment for additional concrete is equitable. In uncertain or variable ground, a Geotechnical Baseline Report (GBR, Chapter 2; ASCE, 2007) establishes expected conditions as the basis of bids, differing site condition assessment and payment, well suited to design-build on highly variable sites (Dwyre et al., 2010).
key_points: Preferred: separate soil and rock excavation pay items (Appendix D); unclassified raises bid contingency
Guide specification divides soil and rock at unconfined compressive strength of 1,000 psi; or by equipment needed
Separate pay item for obstructions (e.g., 2 or 3 times soil rate, time and materials, or a shared-risk quantity)
Concrete by design volume with a contractual overpour allowance where losses (karst) are expected
Geotechnical Baseline Report for uncertain or variable ground (ASCE, 2007)
sections.applicability: Measurement and payment provisions for drilled shafts

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [p. 14-8] Technical specifications addressing the project's specific conditions and requirements are critical; the Appendix D guide specification identifies typical issues and provisions and can be tailored, and the manual's design and construction information should inform the specification.
key_points: Tailor the Appendix D guide specification to the project
Use the manual's design and construction information in writing the specification
sections.applicability: Overview of Chapter 14, Drilled Shaft Construction Specification.
